video_title: Why Abundance Is an Illusion with Jeff Currie | TGS 229
gist: Recorded July 23, 2026, former Goldman Sachs commodities head Jeff Currie argues that refined products, not crude, are where the real shortage already is: the 3-2-1 crack spread at $60/bbl is the highest of his three-decade career after strikes took out roughly half of Russian refining and the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea were all closed. He frames Western policy as an 'abundance illusion' - draining strategic reserves and talking markets down to avoid ever admitting scarcity - which suppresses the price signal needed to trigger investment, and argues the Bretton Woods 'grand bargain' of US-protected sea lanes for dollar usage is breaking, ending globalization and forcing a return to state capitalism. His portfolio conclusion is a rotation between scarcity (oil, copper, ags) and debasement (gold), with capital only arriving after physical shortages appear.

insights.claim: The 3-2-1 crack spread (three parts gasoline, two diesel, one crude) reached $60 a barrel, the highest level Jeff Currie has seen in three decades of covering commodities, implying products priced as if crude were $160 while crude trades near $100.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Refining margins, not flat crude, are where the physical tightness is being expressed - refiner equities and product spreads are the cleaner expression of the shock than long crude.
insights.quote: It's sixty dollars a barrel That's the highest level in the three decades I've been doing this.

insights.claim: Currie treats refined product prices as the true signal of physical tightness and crude as noise, arguing the macro community is watching the wrong instrument.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A reusable screen: when crude and products diverge, position off product cracks and inventories rather than headline Brent/WTI.
insights.quote: I like to say crude is the noise, products are the signal, but their people are not looking at them.

insights.claim: Diesel products are up roughly 81% year to date versus about 34% for the broad commodity index, making diesel the current bottleneck after oil earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The bottleneck rotates within commodities while the return trend persists - track which sub-complex is binding rather than abandoning the asset class.

insights.claim: Ukrainian strikes reaching 1,300 kilometers into Russia have taken out nearly half of Russian refining capacity, forcing the world's supposedly largest product and crude exporter to import jet fuel from Japan and diesel from India.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Russia flipping from product exporter to importer removes a structural supply cushion that global product balances had assumed permanent.

insights.claim: Because Soviet-era Russian refineries have a single crude pipe feeding the CDU, knocking out the refinery also shuts in the upstream crude, with only about 35% of that crude redirectable and roughly eighteen months to rebuild the damaged units.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Refinery damage in Russia is a crude supply loss too, so the bullish product story converts into a bullish crude story with a multi-quarter lag.

insights.claim: China's decision to cut refinery runs and refined product exports and draw down its own product stocks made global products tighter even though observers credited it with keeping prices down for Trump.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The consensus read of Chinese behavior as price-suppressive is backwards for products; watch Chinese refinery run rates as a swing factor in diesel.

insights.claim: Product tankers could not be used to evacuate supply from the Arab Gulf because refined product ships effectively function as bombs when hit, unlike crude tankers which merely catch fire, so crude was shipped instead of the products the market needed.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Wartime shipping physics structurally biases the market toward crude surplus and product deficit - a persistent reason cracks stay elevated.

themes.theme: Hormuz Complacency and the Escalation Trap

insights.claim: Despite the Red Sea, Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz all being disrupted and roughly half of Russian refining destroyed, crude was still struggling to hold $100 a barrel, a combination Currie says would two years ago have implied global recession.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The gap between physical disruption and price is the trade - it implies asymmetric upside if the market is forced to reprice.

insights.claim: Currie argues the conditional probability of oil going to $150 once it clears $100 is now high because inventory buffers are depleted, unlike in prior cycles when the move was gradual.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Call spreads or upside optionality above $100 are mispriced if the distribution is jump-like rather than continuous.
insights.quote: the conditional probability going to 150 once you get over to 100 is pretty high

insights.claim: The market's assumption that Trump will back down is flawed because he has no remaining concession to offer - the MOU was the rabbit he already pulled from the hat, and Iran will not supply crude on those terms again.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The de-escalation put that the macro community is implicitly short is much less valuable than priced.

insights.claim: Currie expects the current Middle East confrontation to be seen in retrospect as a Waterloo-style strategic defeat, with Iran gaining leverage every week that passes.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Positions should be sized for a prolonged, structurally worsening geopolitical premium rather than a resolution trade.
insights.quote: I think this is gonna be, uh, akin to Napoleon's Waterloo in retrospect

insights.claim: Even instant peace would not restore supply, because damaged Middle Eastern and Russian wells have water-cut and restart problems and negotiated supply contracts are being redirected from West to East.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A ceasefire headline is a fade rather than a reason to exit long commodity exposure.

insights.claim: US and allied missile inventories are being drained fighting $40,000 drones with million-dollar Patriot interceptors, a trade Currie says should be replaced by F-15s and F-35s dropping gravity bombs and which he was told leaves the West in a dangerous position.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Munitions restocking is a multi-year defense-industrial demand stream and a further claim on metals and manufacturing capacity.
insights.quote: You cannot fight, um, $40,000 drones with million-dollar Patriot missiles.

themes.theme: The Physical Capital Paradox and State Capitalism

insights.claim: Commodities are the best performing asset class of the decade, up over 200% versus roughly 157% for crypto on average, dating from the bullish supercycle call Currie made in October 2020.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Allocators who dismiss commodities on price-level optics have missed the highest-returning sleeve of the decade.
insights.quote: Commodities are the best performing asset class this decade. You know, you're up over 200%. Crypto on average is 157.

insights.claim: This cycle's commodity returns come from rolling a backwardated front end rather than price appreciation, so being long oil during the war generated about 40% returns even while oil sat near $60 and below its pre-war level.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Judge commodity exposure on total return including roll yield, not spot - a flat or falling price can still pay handsomely.

insights.claim: Energy is just under 4% of the S&P and energy plus basic materials is under 6%, roughly a third of the long-run average, so even a 100% move in energy adds only about 3% to a portfolio while tech at ~50% weight needs just 6% to match it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Explains structural complacency: index-relative managers are rationally uninterested in commodities until an energy shock demolishes their tech-heavy returns as in 2022.

insights.claim: Dodd-Frank removed bank proprietary risk-taking from commodity markets, concentrating roughly 98% of liquidity in the first six months of the curve and leaving no counterparty to sell long-dated hedges, so the only practical way to buy oil 18 months out is to buy an oil company.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The absence of back-end liquidity means physical hedgers must use equities, and it mechanically converts commodity moves into spikes rather than trends.

insights.claim: Without back-end buying, commodity markets hit potholes and spike vertically instead of anticipating them, which Currie illustrates with Gerald Ford's ban on onion futures and with Newcastle coal doing nothing through the whole 2000s supercycle before going straight up in late 2008.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Markets lacking deep forward curves should be traded for gap risk, not trend - a reason to own optionality rather than delta.

insights.claim: Energy companies are throwing off a 15% free cash flow yield, which Currie labels the 'munificent seven', yet capital still will not come until physical shortages and lines appear - as in the 1970s and the 2000s when BHP-type names rose 50x only after warehouse shelves emptied.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The catalyst for the commodity capital rotation is a visible physical shortage, not valuation - wait for empty shelves, then expect a violent flow.
insights.quote: People don't buy these stories until you run out, and then that capital flows.

insights.claim: Currie says state capitalism is back because the needed projects have roughly 27-year durations and billions in upfront cost that private investors will not tolerate, comparing it to the World War II conversion of auto plants into weapons plants.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Expect state-backed financing vehicles and offtake guarantees to become the dominant funding channel for energy and mining - a policy trade as much as a commodity one.
insights.quote: I think state capitalism is back.

insights.claim: Currie traces the Western policy of never admitting scarcity to Jimmy Carter's two 1977 speeches - the cardigan 'conserve' speech that triggered panic and higher prices, and the April speech coining 'energy transition' as the moral equivalent of war, mocked as MEOW.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Explains why policymakers systematically suppress rather than transmit scarcity signals, delaying the investment response and enlarging the eventual spike.
insights.quote: Never admit the scarcity, 'cause he got killed.

insights.claim: Every US president from George H.W. Bush through Trump has run the same abundance illusion - releasing the SPR and talking the market down to bridge to returning supply - and Trump needed it in his second term though not his first.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Reserve releases should be read as a bet on supply returning, not as a bearish fundamental - and the bet fails when the buffer runs out.

insights.claim: Drawing down strategic petroleum reserves liquidates a buffer built over decades in order to suppress the very price signal that would trigger the investment response the market needs.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Policy-suppressed prices mean the supply response is delayed, making the eventual shortage deeper and the price move more violent.

insights.claim: China took Carter's energy transition logic seriously for security rather than environmental reasons and became the world leader in nuclear generation technology, solar, wind, batteries and lithium, which Currie says leaves it in a relatively good position now.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The security framing, not the climate framing, is what mobilizes capital - watch for Western energy policy to be re-labeled as defense spending.
insights.quote: It heeded that advice and invested in it. It had nothing to do with the environment, but everything for energy security

themes.theme: Grand Bargain, Exorbitant Privilege and Bloc Fragmentation

insights.claim: The Bretton Woods grand bargain gave the US exorbitant privilege in exchange for using its navy to protect global sea lanes, and with the Red Sea, Strait of Hormuz and Black Sea all blocked simultaneously that bargain is visibly unfulfilled.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: If the sea-lane guarantee is not restored, the credit flows that fund US consumption and asset prices are the thing at risk, not just oil.

insights.claim: Currie argues that if foreign capital stops trusting the US and pulls out because the grand bargain is broken, the adjustment falls on middle class American living standards.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The transmission channel from geopolitics to US households is capital flight and lost credit access, which argues for owning hard assets over US consumption exposure.
insights.quote: That's gonna hit middle class America and change their lifestyles like they've never seen before.

insights.claim: Trump's derided proposal for a 20% tax on oil transiting the Strait of Hormuz was an attempt to get paid for the expensive service of protecting sea lanes, and Currie's 'New Martiel Plan' argues that once interest rates rose the system became too expensive for any president to maintain.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: The retreat from global policing is rate-driven and structural, so it survives changes of administration - price permanent risk premia into shipping and energy.

insights.claim: Currie frames the current conflict as BRICS versus G7 with Europeans not realizing they are participants, bookending the 1991 Gulf War moment when the Soviet Union fell and the US won overwhelmingly and became the globalization hegemon.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Treat 1991 and 2026 as the open and close of the globalization trade, with the reverse of every asset that benefited from it.
insights.quote: this is BRICS versus G7, even though the Europeans don't know

insights.claim: China controls the world's atoms through critical minerals processing that the West and even the Soviets refused to do domestically, controls the world's molecules through its backing of Iran, and would control the world's chips if it takes Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A single actor holding all three chokepoints makes supply-chain redundancy a national-security capex cycle rather than a corporate choice.
insights.quote: So they control the world's atoms, they control the world's molecules, and also the strait, um, Taiwan to get them into Taiwan, um, then they control the world's chips

insights.claim: Currie's worst realistic case short of nuclear use is Putin choosing to cut the West off from Russian commodities entirely, which he calls a non-trivial probability given Russia is the only one of the three largest producers with both metals and energy while the US has energy without metals and China metals without energy.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A Russian export embargo would shut down Western industrial processes - a tail risk worth hedging in metals rather than only in oil.
insights.quote: Russia has both metals and energy. China has metals, but no energy.

themes.theme: Scarcity Versus Debasement: The Second Supercycle

insights.claim: Currie's framework for the next decade is a rotation between two themes - scarcity, headlined by oil, copper and an agricultural proxy like corn or soybeans, and debasement, headlined by gold.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A simple two-factor allocation map for the decade: rotate between the scarcity basket and the debasement basket rather than picking one.
insights.quote: You're gonna rotate between the thematics of scarcity and debasement.

insights.claim: Currie cites the levels already reached - gold having hit $5,500 and trading around $4,200, diesel at $160, Brent around $101 and copper at $14,000 a ton - and says these are only the foothills of the Himalayas relative to what is coming.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Anchors for how far the complex has already moved and a claim that the distribution of further upside is still fat.
insights.quote: we're only in the foothills of the Himalayas at this point

insights.claim: Supply response is structurally impossible on the relevant timeframe because a copper mine takes roughly twenty years to bring on, no new refineries have been built, and current Brazilian and Guyanese oil growth is the output of the previous investment cycle.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Bearish supply arguments based on current production growth are backward-looking; the forward pipeline is empty.

insights.claim: Goldman's regularly published list of top oil projects had, in its most recent version, no major new projects for the first time ever, a direct legacy of the sustainability-driven halt to oil investment earlier in the decade.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable indicator that the supply cliff is already locked in for the back half of the decade.

insights.claim: The AI build-out represents roughly $800 billion of spending this year with more than 50% flowing directly into commodities - metals, turbines, transformers - against zero incremental investment in the raw materials required.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Currie calls it the biggest demand shock commodities have ever seen and says exaggeratedly that all of it ends up in the price of copper.

insights.claim: Currie sees significant upside in agriculture from the combination of El Nino heat, Black Sea and Odessa port disruption to Russian and Ukrainian grain, a fertilizer shock arriving in 2027, and the exhaustion of the strong-dollar incentive that drove Latin American acreage expansion.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: He owns the whole commodity index rather than only oil precisely because ags and metals carry independent shocks.

insights.claim: Currie concedes peak oil supply may already be upon us because the extent of damage to Russian and Middle Eastern productive capacity is unknown, which would force the electrification transition far faster.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Supply-side peak oil is a live scenario that would compress the energy transition timeline and reprice both oil and battery supply chains.
insights.quote: If you took out Russia and the Middle East, well, folks, you, you better learn how to make those batteries really quick

themes.theme: Fiscal Transfers, Credit and Sovereign Fragility

insights.claim: Currie argues inflation is caused by fiscal transfers to low-income households rather than by monetary policy, noting twenty years of interest rate cuts produced no inflation while Biden-era $2,000 checks made commodity prices explode.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Watch fiscal transfer policy, not the Fed, as the leading indicator for the next commodity-led inflation impulse.
insights.quote: you cut interest rates for 20 years, inflation never materialized. You do fiscal transfers, and you're off to the races.

insights.claim: The mechanism is that the bottom two income quintiles have zero credit and live paycheck to paycheck, so only they increase physical commodity demand when handed cash, whereas a high-income household consumes the same amount of corn regardless.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Gives a testable rule for which policies are commodity-inflationary: cash to the credit-less bottom, not rate cuts to the credit-rich.

insights.claim: Currie argues inflation is actually bad for high-income households rather than low-income ones, because the low earners keep the refrigerator they bought in 2022 while the high earners paid for it through a 27% drawdown in the S&P.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Reframes inflation as a wealth transfer that destroys financial assets, arguing for hard-asset hedges in high-net-worth portfolios.
insights.quote: inflationary is caused by low income people, and it's bad to high income people

insights.claim: Redistribution is Currie's second big structural theme - he says the only way to handle scarcity is fiscal transfers to lower incomes, and that the US K-shaped economy is becoming more extreme, making those transfers politically inevitable and inflationary.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Scarcity plus inequality mechanically produces inflationary policy - a structural tailwind for the commodity complex.

insights.claim: Commodity price levels are set by credit availability rather than physical demand alone, and open interest has fallen because credit is flowing to AI build-outs while little is available for the rest of the global economy.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Explains why physical tightness has not yet produced a clearing price - a credit rotation into commodities would be the accelerant.

insights.claim: Currie says the dangerous imbalance sits on sovereign balance sheets rather than corporate ones, arguing that an AI valuation unwind at companies now worth 40% of the S&P would resemble what oil companies went through in 2014 and be survivable, while sovereign stress would not.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Positions the real tail risk in rates and currencies rather than in tech equity, favoring gold as the debasement hedge.
insights.quote: The real imbalance is sitting on the US government balance sheet.

themes.theme: War Kit 2.0 and the Rise of the Electron State

insights.claim: Currie distinguishes War Kit 1.0, the oil-based 'artificial muscle' military, from War Kit 2.0 built on artificial intelligence, drones and batteries, and says Ukraine and Iran have just demonstrated 1.0 does not work.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Defense procurement shifts from liquid-fuel platforms to batteries and autonomy - a demand reallocation from oil toward electrochemical supply chains.
insights.quote: War Kit 1.0, that's artificial muscle. That was the oil-based war kit. Um, War Kit 2.0 is artificial intelligence. That's drones, um, and AI.

insights.claim: Large fuel-carrying assets - aerial refuelers, product tankers, B1 bombers - are now sitting targets for cheap drones, so militaries need concealable battery power instead, making battery technology the decisive race.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: Battery capability becomes a defense imperative rather than a climate one, which is how it gets funded at scale.

insights.claim: Currie is bullish on Europe: 81% debt to GDP versus 125% for the US and near 300% for China, greater income equality, protected consumer surplus and rule of law, plus French nuclear and German renewables - with battery technology the one missing piece.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A contrarian long-Europe case tied explicitly to whether Europe can acquire battery technology while spending 5% of GDP on the new war kit.

insights.claim: Currie names ASML rather than Nvidia or TSMC as the company with the biggest moat in the AI stack, reinforcing his view that Europe holds a dominant position even in the AI race.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable European equity expression of the AI and deglobalization theme.
insights.quote: which of the three big companies, Nvidia, ASML, or TSMC is the most dominant one? Well, who has the biggest moat? ASML has it.

insights.claim: Currie's core electrification argument is that coal, gas and oil carry a marginal cost of consumption while renewables, batteries and nuclear have zero, so whoever front-loads the sunk capital - China - runs its data centers, models and robots on zero-marginal-cost power and wins, analogous to America building the transcontinental railroads.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: If correct, the AI race is decided by electricity cost structure rather than chips, making Chinese power buildout the variable to track.
insights.quote: coal, gas, and oil have a marginal cost of consumption Renewables, batteries, and nuclear power have zero.

insights.claim: Currie argues electrification can reach 80% of energy use from today's roughly 20% by leaving aside cement, jet fuel and similar hard-to-abate uses, and that peak oil demand will be turbocharged now that the driver is security rather than environmentalism - though he insists it is not tomorrow and heavy oil investment is still required.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: A world splitting into petro states and electron states creates a divergence trade between long-dated oil assets and electrification supply chains.

insights.claim: The AI build-out moves the technology sector from infinitely scalable zero-marginal-cost software to steel-in-the-ground businesses with upward sloping supply curves, which Currie says he already experiences as compute constraints on his own Claude Max subscription and predicts will force fixed-fee AI pricing to explode.
insights.speaker: Jeff Currie
insights.so_what: AI unit economics deteriorate as physical inputs bind, which is both a margin risk for hyperscalers and confirmation of the commodity demand thesis.
